---
title: "Finding unobserved groups"
---

Some linguistic datasets provide measurements without a group label that should be predicted. A speaker may be represented by language-use ratings. A language may be represented by grammatical features. A vowel token may be represented by formant measurements. The [unit of analysis](../foundations/linguistic-data.qmd) still determines what can be grouped. We may then ask whether the represented objects form recurring groups.

The group is unobserved in the limited sense that it is not supplied as a response variable to the fitting procedure. The measurements are observed, and any later linguistic interpretation still requires evidence outside the fitted partition.

## Two kinds of group representation

The module develops two ways to estimate groups that are not supplied as response labels.

1. K-means clustering assigns every object to exactly one cluster.
2. A [**finite mixture model**](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/finite-mixtures.html) gives every object a model-based posterior probability for each component.

The second representation is not automatically better. It answers a different question and makes a more detailed distributional commitment.

## The K-means branch

We begin with [representing objects](representing-objects.qmd), because a group can only reflect the rows and columns supplied to the analysis. [Distance and scaling](distance-and-scaling.qmd) then define what it means for two represented objects to be close.

[K-means](k-means.qmd) introduces cluster assignments and derives its assignment and centroid updates. [Within-cluster loss](within-cluster-loss.qmd) describes fitted compactness across candidate group counts. [Silhouette widths](silhouette-scores.qmd) compare each row with its assigned group and nearest alternative. [Validation without labels](unsupervised-validation.qmd) then asks whether centroids fit on training rows represent rows excluded from fitting.

## The probabilistic-mixture branch

[Gaussian mixtures](gaussian-mixtures.qmd) replace distance to one centroid with a probability model for several component distributions. [Posterior membership](posterior-membership.qmd) turns weighted component densities into membership probabilities. [Expectation-maximization](expectation-maximization.qmd) alternates membership and parameter updates to fit the model. [Choosing a mixture with BIC](choosing-a-mixture.qmd) penalizes fitted likelihood for parameter count. [Held-out mixture validation](validating-a-mixture.qmd) then asks whether the fitted density transfers to new speakers.

The Peterson and Barney vowel measurements provide the sustained phonetic application for this branch. The application is useful because formant distributions overlap, speaker anatomy affects the raw representation, and intended vowel labels can be reserved for interpretation rather than supplied to the mixture.

## What a learned group can establish

A fitted group is a summary under a declared representation, distance, or probability model. It is not automatically a phoneme, dialect, speaker type, or language type. Agreement with an external annotation may support an interpretation, but the annotation did not define the fitted objective.

The statistical object is a partition or component distribution. Interpreting it as a linguistic category requires a separate substantive claim about the process that produced the measurements.

By the end of the module, we should be able to reconstruct each fitted quantity, identify the assumptions that create the groups, and state which additional evidence would be needed to interpret them linguistically.
